notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Why a model id is a moving target unless you pin it — Anthropic: model deprecations

  • What a change to any one component does to the others — Anthropic: demystifying evals for AI agents

  • Versioning the harness alongside the model — Harness engineering: agent = model + harness

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • versioning and rollout — versioning strategies and rollout mechanics.

  • Versioning & rollout — the LLMOps view of the same.

What this note adds: the coupling argument, with the arithmetic. Four components that version independently produce a combination space you cannot evaluate — and an eval only ever validates a combination, which is what forces the four into one artifact.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What the eval actually validates? One combination of prompt, tools, model and graph.
Combinations at 3 versions each? 81 — of which you tested one.
Why a floating model alias is the worst case? Your artifact changes with no deploy, no eval, no rollback target.
What a tool description change breaks? Selection for tools you didn't touch.
What rollback must restore? All four together — anything less isn't the tested state.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I version the four together as one artifact, because the eval suite can only ever bless a combination and shipping them independently means running a combination nobody measured. The prompt is tuned against a model; a tool description changes selection for tools you didn't edit; the graph decides when each is reached. Pinning the model id is the non-negotiable part — a floating alias means the provider can change my system without a deploy, so there's nothing to roll back to and no record of what was running. The pivot is cadence: coupling slows down the copy-fix-sized changes, and the answer there is a fast path for changes the eval trigger says can't move behaviour, not four independent version numbers.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Four independent versions Never in production. An untested combination in production, and no rollback target. Prompt in one repo, model id in a deploy config, tools in a registry.
One coupled artifact Anything you evaluate. The default. Small changes carry the whole release ceremony. A change to any one of them moves behaviour on tasks it doesn't mention.
Coupled, with a declared fast path Mature pipeline, high change rate. You must define — and defend — what "can't move behaviour" means. Copy fixes queueing behind a full suite.
Floating model alias Never. The provider deploys to you, silently. A model name with latest in it.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Independent Nothing — which is why it happens. None. "What was running on Tuesday" is unanswerable.
Coupled artifact A manifest holding prompt hash, tool schema hash, model id and graph version. One eval run per release rather than per component. Rollback is one identifier; traces name the artifact version.
Fast path A classifier over changed files, tied to the eval triggers. Cheap changes stay cheap. The fast path becomes the thing people abuse when in a hurry.
Floating alias None. None. Silent behaviour change; the incident timeline has no deploy in it.

The manifest is the whole architectural change, and it's small: four identifiers in one file, emitted onto every trace. What it buys is that a regression report, an eval result and a production trace can all name the same thing — without it, correlating them is reconstruction rather than lookup.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

Why independent versioning is untestable. With c components each having v deployed versions, the number of distinct running combinations is:

combinations = v ᶜ

Four components at three versions each is 81 combinations. Your eval suite ran against one of them. The other 80 are configurations that exist, can reach production through ordinary independent deploys, and have never been measured. Coupling doesn't reduce the risk by being careful — it reduces the space from 81 to 1 by construction.

Why the coupling is real and not bureaucratic. Each pair genuinely interacts:

  • prompt × model — instructions are tuned to a model's tendencies; a version bump changes tool-calling format adherence and verbosity
  • tools × prompt — a tool description is part of the prompt the model sees, so editing one tool changes selection among all of them
  • graph × prompt — the graph decides what context a prompt is reached with
  • model × tools — parallel-call behaviour and schema strictness differ by model version

None of these are visible in a diff. A reviewer reading a one-line tool description change has no way to see that it moved selection on a different tool, which is why the answer is a suite run against the whole combination rather than a more careful review.

What pinning actually prevents. A floating alias resolves to whatever the provider currently points it at. The consequences compound: the running system differs from the evaluated one; a behaviour change has no corresponding deploy in the timeline, so the incident investigation starts by ruling out your own changes; and there is no previous version to roll back to, because the rollback target was never a version you named. Pinning turns a provider-side change into an ordinary deploy you schedule, evaluate and can reverse.

The cost of coupling, quantified honestly. If the expensive eval suite takes an hour and a team ships ten changes a day, coupling every change costs ten hours of pipeline. That's the real objection, and the answer is a declared fast path rather than independent versions: changes that touch none of the four behaviour-affecting inputs skip the suite and still ship as a new artifact version. The artifact stays coupled; only the validation is tiered.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

The pinning check sits above the eval rather than beside it because an unpinned model makes every downstream result provisional — you can run the suite, pass it, and be running something else by the afternoon. It's the one branch in this diagram that invalidates the others rather than adding to them.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "Quality dropped on a Tuesday. We'd shipped nothing for nine days."

Root cause. The model was configured by an alias that tracked the latest snapshot, chosen during the prototype so the team would automatically get improvements. The provider rolled a new snapshot behind that alias. The system prompt had been tuned over months against the old one — several instructions existed specifically to suppress behaviours the old snapshot had — and against the new one those instructions were counterproductive. No deploy appeared in the timeline, so the first two days of investigation went to infrastructure and to a dependency that had been upgraded in the same window and was innocent.

Fix. The model id was pinned to an explicit snapshot and added to the artifact manifest alongside the prompt hash, the tool schema hash and the graph version, with the manifest id emitted on every trace. Upgrades became scheduled changes with an eval run and a rollback target. The late cost was the two days, plus re-tuning the prompt for the new snapshot with no baseline to compare against — the old snapshot's behaviour was no longer reproducible, so the comparison everyone wanted could not be run.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why can't the prompt version independently? It's just text.

Because its meaning is a function of the model reading it and the tools it describes. An instruction that reliably suppresses a behaviour on one model snapshot may do nothing on the next, and a prompt that lists tools is invalidated the moment a tool's schema changes. The text is versionable; what the text does is a property of the combination.

The practical test is what a rollback restores. If a prompt regression is fixed by reverting the prompt alone, you've restored the prompt to a state that was evaluated against a possibly different model and tool set — so you're now in a combination nobody measured, reached by an action everyone believed was safe.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Coupling slows everything down. How do you keep a fast change fast?

By tiering the validation rather than the artifact. Every change still produces a new artifact version with all four identifiers in it, so the running state is always nameable and reversible. What varies is what has to pass before it ships: a change touching none of the behaviour-affecting inputs runs deterministic checks and goes, and a change touching any of them runs the expensive suite.

The discipline that makes it work is that the fast path is defined by the inputs it touches, not by the author's judgement of risk. "This is just a copy fix" is exactly how a prompt edit ships unevaluated. A file-path or manifest-diff rule is boring and it doesn't get talked into anything.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

What happens when a provider deprecates the snapshot you pinned?

You get a deadline rather than a surprise, which is the whole benefit. Deprecation notices come with dates, so the migration becomes a planned piece of work: run the suite on the new snapshot, see the delta, re-tune whatever moved, ship it as an artifact version with a rollback target that still works until the old snapshot is actually retired.

The scaling version of this problem is having many pinned artifacts — several agents, each on a different snapshot, each with prompts tuned to it. That's real maintenance and it's an argument for consolidating onto few model versions deliberately, rather than for floating. Floating doesn't remove the migration work, it just performs it for you at a time you didn't choose and without the suite.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design versioning for a platform where tenants supply their own prompts.

The artifact splits in two, and saying so is most of the answer. The platform artifact holds the model id, the tool schemas and the graph; the tenant artifact holds their prompt and their tool selections. Each versions independently because they're owned by different people — but every run records both ids, so the combination is still nameable after the fact even though nobody validated it in advance.

That leaves the platform with a real obligation: a model version bump changes the combination for every tenant prompt, none of which the platform has evaluated. So the upgrade needs a shadow run across a sampled corpus of real tenant traffic before it lands, and tenants need advance notice and ideally a window where they can test against the new version themselves.

The part I'd raise unprompted is that this makes the model version a public API. Once tenants tune prompts against a snapshot, changing it is a breaking change to their product, and the platform either pins per tenant — expensive, and it fragments the fleet — or commits to a deprecation policy with notice periods. That's a product decision made at deployment-design time, and it's much cheaper to decide now than after the first tenant's prompt breaks.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "We version prompts in git, so prompt changes are tracked."

✅ Reality: Tracked, not validated. A prompt version is only meaningful with the model and tools it was evaluated against — four components at three versions is 81 combinations, and your suite blessed one.

❌ Trap: "We use the latest model alias so we automatically get improvements."

✅ Reality: You also automatically get regressions, with no deploy in the timeline and no rollback target. The provider becomes an unreviewed committer to your system.

❌ Trap: "Rolling back the prompt fixes a prompt regression."

✅ Reality: Only if the other three are where they were when that prompt was evaluated. Otherwise the rollback lands in a fresh untested combination, which is why the artifact is the rollback unit.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • versioning and rollout — the versioning mechanics.

  • Versioning & rollout — the LLMOps framing.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §13 How a rollout knows it's working — the artifact is what a canary compares.

  • §12 What blocks the merge — the model id being a gated input is this note's pinning rule enforced in CI.

  • §12 What a span must carry — the artifact version belongs on every span.

  • §11 Where the approval gate sits — tool schema changes are versioned here and audited there.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Multi-tenant agent platform — the two-artifact split above is the design.

  • §14 Coding agent — prompts tuned hard to one model make pinning load-bearing.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The acceleration limits a fast ramp trips, which look like a regression — Anthropic: rate limits

  • Judging a rollout on task success rather than on health checks — Anthropic: demystifying evals for AI agents

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • versioning and rollout — shadow runs, canaries, flags and rollback.

What this note adds: the sample-size constraint. An agent regression returns HTTP 200, so the canary's verdict is a statistical comparison — and that fixes how long the canary must run, which is the number nobody computes before promising a same-day rollout.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Why error rate is a useless canary signal? A worse agent still returns 200 with a plausible answer.
What sets canary duration? Trials needed for significance ÷ the share of traffic you gave it.
What a shadow run must not have? Live write tools — neuter them or it acts twice.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

The thing that makes agent rollout different is that a regression isn't an error — the new version returns 200s with slightly worse answers, so latency and error-rate dashboards stay green while quality drops. That means the canary has to be judged on a task-success signal, and a task-success signal is a proportion, so promoting needs enough runs to be significant. I work that backwards before committing to a schedule: detecting a five-point drop takes a few hundred runs per arm, so a canary on 5% of traffic needs however long 5% takes to produce them. Shadow runs come first where I can afford them, because they catch crashes and cost regressions with no user exposure — provided the write tools are neutered, or the shadow performs every action twice.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Shadow run Before any user exposure. Doubles cost; catches quality only if you grade both outputs. Write tools that can be stubbed cleanly.
Canary on task success The main promotion gate. Duration set by statistics, not by preference. Enough traffic to reach significance in hours.
Flag-gated cohort Low traffic, or a tenant who agreed to be early. Not a random sample — that cohort isn't the population. Design partners, or internal users first.
Straight deploy with fast rollback Low stakes, or traffic too thin for statistics. Users are the detector. A few hundred runs a day total.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Shadow Traffic duplication, and a switch that disables effectful tools on the shadow path. Double model spend for the window. Compare cost and step count per run; quality needs a judge on both.
Canary Traffic splitting by artifact version, and an online success metric. A fraction of traffic on the new version. A promotion rule with a number in it, and a defined bake time.
Flag cohort A flag service and cohort assignment. Minimal. Fast signal from a biased sample — good for crashes, weak for quality.
Straight deploy None. None. Rollback speed is the only control that matters.

The duration arithmetic. A canary compares two proportions, so the trials needed scale with p(1−p)/d² for a detectable difference d. Resolving a five-point drop around 80% success takes a few hundred runs per arm. At 10,000 runs a day and a 5% canary, the canary sees 500 runs a day — so the honest bake time is about a day, not the twenty minutes the deploy pipeline implies. Halving the detectable difference quadruples the wait.

The pairing shortcut doesn't apply here. Offline you cut variance by running both versions on the same tasks; in a canary the arms see different live traffic, so task-mix difference is variance you can't cancel. Canary numbers are noisier than eval numbers at the same sample size, which makes a canary a safety net rather than a replacement for the offline suite.

Ramp gradually, because the provider notices. Sharp increases in usage can trip acceleration limits and return 429s independently of your configured rate limits. A canary promoted from 5% to 100% in one step can produce exactly the error spike that looks like the new version failing, when the cause is the shape of the ramp.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "The canary was green for an hour so we promoted, and escalations doubled the next day."

Root cause. The promotion rule was "no increase in error rate or p95 latency over one hour at 5% traffic" — a sensible rule for a stateless service and meaningless for an agent. The new artifact returned 200s at normal latency and resolved fewer tickets, which is invisible to both signals. At 5% of traffic for an hour, the canary had also seen about twenty runs, which could not have detected a twenty-point drop, let alone the eight-point one that shipped.

Fix. The promotion rule moved to escalation rate over a bake window derived from the traffic share and the difference worth catching — about a day at that volume — with error rate and latency demoted to abort conditions rather than promotion criteria. The late cost was a day of doubled escalations absorbed by the support team, and a rollback that was itself risky because a day of runs had already written state under the new version.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • versioning and rollout — the rollout mechanisms.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §13 What the versioned unit is — the artifact is what the canary compares and what rollback restores.

  • §12 Which production signal you're willing to treat as a label — the canary's verdict comes from there.

  • §12 What blocks the merge — the offline gate and the canary catch different regressions.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — escalation rate is both the canary signal and the business metric.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Provider-side concurrency ceilings the autoscaler must respect — Anthropic: rate limits

  • Why agent workers hold state and connections that fight scale-in — Langfuse: observability SDK

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • deployment and scaling — stateless workers, external state, autoscaling shapes.

  • concurrency and parallelism — concurrency in agent systems.

What this note adds: the wrong-signal problem. An agent worker spends nearly all of a run blocked on the model, so CPU stays near zero while the worker is fully occupied — which makes the default autoscaling signal actively misleading, and Little's Law gives the right one.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Why CPU is the wrong signal? Runs are I/O-bound; CPU is idle while the worker is full.
The right signal? In-flight runs against a concurrency limit, or queue depth.
What Little's Law gives you? Concurrency L = λW — arrival rate × run duration.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Agent workers are the case where the default autoscaling signal lies. A run spends almost all its wall-clock waiting on model and tool responses, so CPU sits near idle while the worker is holding as many runs as it can — scale on CPU and you scale down under load. I scale on in-flight runs against a declared concurrency limit, or on queue depth where work is queued, and I size capacity from Little's Law rather than from observation. The other half is that scale-in must not kill work: state lives outside the worker and the run checkpoints, so a terminating instance drains rather than drops, and the client's connection is decoupled from whichever worker is executing.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Scale on CPU Never for agent workers. Scales the wrong way — idle CPU under full load. Autoscaler default nobody changed.
Scale on in-flight runs Synchronous request-shaped traffic. The default. You must declare a per-worker concurrency limit and mean it. Runs arrive as requests and someone waits.
Scale on queue depth Async or bursty work. Queue latency becomes the user-facing number. Work is submitted, not awaited.
Fixed capacity Provider limits bind before your compute does. Pays for idle; simple and predictable. ITPM is the ceiling, not CPU.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
In-flight runs A concurrency semaphore per worker, exported as a metric. Tracks load properly. Scale-out reacts to occupancy rather than to a proxy for it.
Queue depth A queue, and a drain policy on shutdown. Absorbs bursts instead of provisioning for them. Queue age becomes the SLO; backpressure becomes a decision.
State outside the worker Checkpoints in a store; the worker holds nothing durable. Storage, and a write per checkpoint. Scale-in drains safely; a killed instance loses nothing.
Decoupled connection A stream broker between client and worker. An extra hop. A worker can be replaced mid-run without dropping the client.

Sizing from Little's Law. Concurrency is arrival rate times duration:

L = λ × W

At 10 runs per second and a 30-second mean run, L = 300 runs in flight. You need capacity for 300 concurrent runs regardless of what CPU says — and if each worker declares a limit of 50, that's six workers, a number derived rather than discovered during an incident. It also shows why run duration is a capacity lever: halving W halves the fleet.

Why the connection is a separate problem. Streaming ties a client to a worker for the length of a run, so a deploy either waits for every run to finish or drops connections mid-stream. Putting a broker between them means the worker is replaceable and the client's stream survives — the same decoupling §9 argues for on latency grounds, reached here from deployment.

Know which ceiling binds. Provider limits are per model on requests, input tokens and output tokens per minute. If ITPM binds before your compute does, autoscaling workers adds queueing rather than throughput, and the fix is upstream — caching, routing, or a limit increase — not more instances.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "Under peak load the autoscaler scaled the fleet down."

Root cause. The workers ran on the platform's default target-tracking policy at 60% CPU. Agent runs are almost entirely waiting on the model, so even at full occupancy the workers sat around 8% CPU. The autoscaler read that as over-provisioning and removed instances, which pushed more runs onto the survivors, which did not raise CPU — so it removed more. Each termination also killed the runs in flight on that instance, because run state lived in worker memory.

Fix. Scaling moved to a custom metric of in-flight runs against a declared per-worker limit, and run state moved to a checkpoint store so that termination drained instead of dropping. The late cost was the state migration: the loop had been written assuming its variables survived, so making a run resumable meant reshaping the harness rather than adding a store — which is why this is a decision to make before the first deploy, not after the first peak.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • deployment and scaling — the scaling shapes.

  • statefulness and persistence — why state leaves the worker.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §13 Which traffic gets the tokens when the provider says no — the ceiling that may bind before compute does.

  • §7 What a checkpoint contains — what makes scale-in safe.

  • §9 Which transport carries the agent's stream — the decoupling, from the latency side.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Deep research agent — long runs make W large, so concurrency dominates capacity.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The three limit dimensions, the token-bucket behaviour, and what counts toward ITPM — Anthropic: rate limits

  • The cache multipliers behind the throughput result below — Anthropic: prompt caching

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Rate limiting quota & API-level multi-tenancy — token buckets, quotas and tenancy at the API layer.

What this note adds: which ceiling actually binds, and the lever nobody counts. Agent throughput is limited by input tokens per minute long before requests per minute — and because cache reads don't count toward that limit, prompt caching is a throughput decision as much as a cost one.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Which ceiling binds first for agents? ITPM — context re-billing consumes it far faster than RPM.
The lever nobody counts? Cache reads don't count toward ITPM; caching multiplies throughput.
Two kinds of 429? Rate limit, with retry-after; spend cap, without one.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

The ceiling that binds an agent is input tokens per minute, not requests — an agent re-sends its whole context every step, so one run burns a large share of the budget while making only twenty requests. The non-obvious part is that cache reads don't count toward the input-token limit, so prompt caching raises effective throughput by roughly the same factor it cuts cost: on a realistic run that's about ten times more runs per minute on an unchanged limit. Beyond that it's allocation. I put a priority queue in the gateway so interactive traffic outranks batch, and carve reserved capacity with per-workspace limits so one feature can't drain the org's budget.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Retry on 429 and hope Never past a prototype. Retries consume the same exhausted budget; latency spikes. An SDK's default retry as the whole strategy.
Cache aggressively first Always — before asking for more limit. Prompt-layout discipline. Cache hit rate near zero and ITPM saturated.
Priority queue in the gateway Mixed interactive and batch traffic. A queue and a classification of traffic. A nightly job starving the product at 2am.
Reserved capacity per workspace Multi-feature or multi-tenant. Reserved headroom sits idle when that tenant is quiet. One feature's spike degrading every other.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Caching for throughput Prompt layout and breakpoint policy. Cuts cost and raises throughput together. Cache hit rate becomes a capacity metric, not just a cost one.
Priority queue A queue with classes in front of the provider client. None. Batch work gets a latency SLO; interactive gets protected.
Reserved capacity Per-workspace limits configured at the provider. Idle reservations. A spike is contained to the workspace that caused it.
Blind retry None. Wasted tokens on rejected calls. A feedback loop that makes exhaustion worse.

Why ITPM binds first, with the numbers. Take the worked run from §10: 20 steps, 365,000 total input tokens. On a 5,000,000 ITPM limit:

uncached:  5,000,000 / 365,000  ≈  13.7 runs per minute

The same run makes 20 requests, so against a 5,000 RPM limit it would support 250 runs per minute. ITPM binds roughly eighteen times sooner than RPM — which is why capacity planning done in requests per second produces a number that is wrong by an order of magnitude.

The throughput lever hiding in the cache. For most models, cache_read_input_tokens do not count toward ITPM; only input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens do. With incremental caching, that same run writes about 34,000 tokens and reads the remaining 331,000:

cached:  5,000,000 / 34,000  ≈  147 runs per minute

A 10.7× throughput increase on an unchanged limit, from the feature you were enabling for cost reasons anyway. It also moves the bottleneck: at 147 runs per minute, RPM at 250 is the same order, so the next capacity conversation is a different one.

Two 429s that need different handling. A rate-limit 429 carries retry-after and retrying works. A spend-cap 429 carries none and is terminal until the cap resets or is raised — retrying, including the SDK's automatic retries, fails every time. Treating them alike turns a budget stop into a retry storm, so the client branches on the error detail, not the status code.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "Every morning at 9am the assistant started failing, and nothing had changed."

Root cause. A nightly enrichment job had grown to overlap the start of the working day. It and the interactive agent shared one API key and therefore one ITPM budget, and the enrichment job's requests were large-context, so it consumed the organisation's input-token budget at a rate its modest request count concealed. Capacity had been planned in requests per second, where the job looked negligible. Interactive traffic met 429s, the client retried into the same exhausted bucket, and latency collapsed.

Fix. The two moved to separate workspaces with their own limits, so the batch job could exhaust its own allocation and nothing else, and a priority queue in the gateway put interactive traffic ahead of batch on the shared path. Enabling prompt caching on the interactive agent afterwards bought back roughly an order of magnitude of headroom, which turned a capacity request into a configuration change.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Rate limiting quota & API-level multi-tenancy — the quota mechanisms.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §10 Which cache tier, and where each one stops being safe — the same caching decision, priced there and throughput-valued here.

  • §10 Where the spend cap is enforced — the other 429, and why they branch differently.

  • §13 What you scale on — when this ceiling binds, adding workers adds queueing.

  • §7 What the queue does when it can't keep up — where rejected work goes.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Multi-tenant agent platform — per-workspace reservations are the isolation story for capacity.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • A standard trace shape, which is the cheapest seam to keep — OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions

  • The self-host versus API framing this note assumes — Anthropic: pricing

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • build vs buy — the build-versus-buy analysis.

  • Self-hosted vs API — build vs buy — the same for inference.

What this note adds: the reversibility half. §2 decides whether to adopt a managed runtime; this decides what you keep portable so that decision can be revisited — and prices the exit per layer, because they differ enormously.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Cheapest seam to keep? Standard trace shape and your own tool interfaces.
Most expensive lock-in? The state and memory model — behaviour comes to depend on it.
The test that keeps it honest? A migration drill, run once, before you need it.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Buying is usually right early, so the interesting decision isn't whether — it's which seams keep it a decision rather than a fact. I rank layers by exit cost. The SDK is cheap to leave and everyone worries about it. Tracing stays portable almost free if you emit a standard span shape. Tools stay mine behind my own interfaces, because that's where the domain logic lives. The expensive one is state and memory: once behaviour depends on how the platform shapes and recalls context, that's a rebuild rather than a port — so if I defend one seam, it's that one.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
No seam — use it natively A genuine prototype with a deadline. Full rewrite to leave; the platform's roadmap becomes yours. Platform types threaded through business logic.
Seam at tools and tracing Default when adopting a platform. A thin interface layer nobody enjoys writing. Domain logic worth more than the orchestration around it.
Seam at state as well You expect to outgrow it, or tenancy is unusual. You reimplement the part the platform was best at. Memory and session shape is becoming product behaviour.
Full abstraction over everything Rarely — usually premature. You build a platform to avoid depending on one. An internal framework nobody asked for.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
No seam Fastest to build. Cheapest now. Pricing changes and deprecations are non-negotiable.
Tools + tracing seam Your interfaces in front of their SDK; standard spans. Marginal. Backend and framework become replaceable decisions.
State seam too Your own checkpoint and memory contract over their store. Real engineering. You own the hardest part, and can move.
Full abstraction A framework, with its own bugs and docs. The most expensive option. Two systems to learn instead of one.

Exit cost per layer, roughly ordered. SDK calls — mechanical, a week, and the layer everyone frets about. Tracing — free if you emitted standard spans, a rewrite if you used bespoke vendor calls. Tools — free if they sit behind your interfaces, since the platform only ever called them. State and memory — the expensive one, because prompts, evals and observed behaviour all encode assumptions about what the platform remembered and how it summarised. There's no adapter for that, only a re-tune and a fresh eval baseline.

The drill is what makes the plan real. A portability claim nobody has tested is a hope. Standing the agent up against a second backend — crude, once, even only the trace exporter and one tool — turns "we could move" into a known quantity and usually finds the two places a platform type leaked into business logic. Run it while leaving is hypothetical; the version run under pricing pressure is much worse.

Why the exit matters even if you never take it. The seam's value is negotiating position, not migration. A team that knows it could move in a quarter behaves differently about a price change or a deprecation than one that knows it can't — and that optionality costs a thin interface layer written at the start.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "The platform deprecated the memory API we'd built on, with six months' notice, and we needed nine."

Root cause. Adoption had been deliberate and the SDK was wrapped — the team had thought about lock-in and addressed the layer they'd read about. The state model wasn't: the platform's session store handled summarisation and recall, and over a year the prompts, eval baselines and tuned context budget all came to assume its behaviour. Replacing it wasn't porting an interface, it was re-deriving what the agent should remember, so every prompt tuned against the old recall had to be re-tuned and re-evaluated.

Fix. A checkpoint and memory contract of their own, with the platform behind it, and the eval suite re-baselined against the new behaviour. The late cost was the three-month overrun and a quarter with no feature work. The cheap version of this fix — the same contract, written at adoption time when nothing depended on it yet — would have been a couple of weeks.
